public_rationale: The claim is universal: every user of every AI subscription service has their tokens subsidized. Anthropic's S-1, as reported, shows that in the first half of 2026 it spent about $2.4 billion serving all paying customers, API and subscriptions together. Subscription revenue alone was about $3.2 billion. So whatever share of serving cost went to subscribers, they paid more as a group than it cost to serve them. If the group pays more than its cost, some subscribers must have covered their own token cost. That breaks 'every single user.' Heavy users, like the Copilot cases he cites, may well be subsidized. And flat-rate plans can hide what each prompt costs. But the universal claim fails for at least one major service.
limitations: The S-1 figures were read through secondary reports, not the filing itself.
The result depends on reading 'subsidized' as paying less than serving cost. On a full-cost reading that includes training, the result could differ.
How costs are split between cost of revenue and R&D is disputed.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Every user of every AI subscription service has their tokens subsidized, and the actual cost of AI is hidden from them.

statement.excerpt: Every single user of every single AI subscription service is having their tokens subsidized and the actual cost of AI obfuscated.

from_speaker: of every single AI subscription service
and the actual cost of AI obfuscated
our_interpretation: 'Subsidized' is read plainly: the provider spends more serving a subscriber's tokens than the subscriber pays. The sentence ties the subsidy to tokens and contrasts it with 'the actual cost of AI', so the actual serving cost is the yardstick, not API list prices.

The claim is universal ('every single user of every single'). If one major service's subscribers as a group pay more than the cost of serving them, at least some subscribers are not subsidized, and the universal claim fails.

Target period: the claim describes an ongoing state around the June 2026 post. I use the first half of 2026 (January–June). That covers the run-up to the post and the June GitHub Copilot billing change he discusses, and it is the nearest period with later-reported cost data.
criteria.support_condition: Would be supported if, for the period, every AI subscription service served its subscribers at a cost above what they paid, so that no subscriber covered their token cost, and the actual costs were hidden.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Would be contradicted if any major AI subscription service's subscribers, as a group, paid more than the cost of serving them in the period. Then at least some subscribers were not subsidized.
